content: Sodium citrate is the sodium salt derived from citric acid, with the chemical formula Na₃C₆H₅O₇. It has a saline and mildly tart flavor. Sodium citrate, along with calcium citrate, is often referred to as sour salt, although this term is sometimes mistakenly applied to citric acid itself. Sodium citrate is primarily used as a food additive, serving as a flavoring agent or preservative. It is commonly employed to enhance the flavor of certain types of club soda. Additionally, it is a frequent ingredient in lemon-lime and citrus-flavored soft drinks, such as Ting, where it contributes to their tart taste. It is also found in energy drinks like Rockstar and Red Bull. In 1914, Belgian physician Albert Hustin and Argentine physician and researcher Luis Agote successfully utilized sodium citrate as an anticoagulant in blood transfusions. This application remains relevant today, as sodium citrate is used in blood collection tubes and for preserving blood in blood banks. The citrate ion works by chelating calcium ions in the blood, thereby disrupting the blood clotting process. As the conjugate base of a weak acid, citrate functions as a buffering agent, helping to stabilize pH levels. Sodium citrate is used to regulate acidity in various substances, such as gelatin desserts. It is also present in mini milk containers often used with coffee machines. Furthermore, it is a byproduct of antacids like Alka-Seltzer when dissolved in water. Recent research by Oopvik et al. demonstrated that consuming approximately 37 grams of sodium citrate improved running performance over a 5-kilometer distance by 30 seconds. Sodium citrate is also used in medical applications to alleviate discomfort associated with urinary tract infections, such as cystitis, to reduce acidosis in conditions like distal renal tubular acidosis, and as an osmotic laxative. In culinary applications, chef Heston Blumenthal utilized sodium citrate as a key ingredient in his television series In Search of Perfection to create cheese slices.
